# Day 36: Why the Smith chart is round

- Date: Wednesday, September 9, 2026
- Block: RF
- Index: https://hardware.ellietaghavi.com/llm/index.md

## Equipment needed

*   Computer with an interactive Smith chart tool (e.g., an online simulator or software)

## Prerequisites

*   [Day 35](https://hardware.ellietaghavi.com/llm/day-35.md) (S11 and Reflection Coefficient).
*   Understanding of complex impedance ($Z = R + jX$).

## Introduction & background

The Smith Chart is the ultimate graphical calculator for RF engineering. It plots complex impedance ($Z = R + jX$) in a way that makes transmission line math intuitive. Because the reflection coefficient $\Gamma$ can never have a magnitude greater than 1 (unless you are dealing with active gain components), mapping the infinite Cartesian impedance plane onto the complex $\Gamma$ plane forces everything into a bounded circle. Moving physically along a transmission line corresponds to rotating perfectly around the center of this chart.

## Core equations

Reflection Coefficient Mapping:
$$\Gamma = \frac{Z_L - Z_0}{Z_L + Z_0}$$

## What you're building

1. A digital mapping exercise charting five complex impedances (50, 25, 100, 50+j50, 50−j50 Ω) onto a digital Smith chart.
2. A theoretical simulation rotating the 50+j50 Ω point through a $0.1\lambda$ transmission line to predict its new impedance landing spot mathematically before the software draws it.

## Activity

Open an interactive Smith chart tool. Plot 50, 25, 100, 50+j50, and 50−j50 Ω; say which neighborhood each lives in (inductive top half, capacitive bottom, R along the axis). Rotate 50+j50 through 0.1λ of 50 Ω line — predict the landing spot before the tool draws it.

## Question to answer

1. What quantity is the chart actually plotting ($\Gamma$ on the complex plane)?
2. Why does $|\Gamma| \le 1$ force everything into a disc?
